source.title: SIGUA: Forgetting May Make Learning with Noisy Labels More Robust
source.authors: Bo Han; Gang Niu; Xingrui Yu; Quanming Yao; Miao Xu; I. Tsang; Masashi Sugiyama

page_placements.theme: Modified training can suppress or reverse corrupted-target fitting

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports training curves and explicit descriptions of learning patterns before accuracy declines under noisy labels. It does not reproduce the original random-label experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper's 80% symmetric-noise demonstration uses true labels to define good and bad data and deliberately changes those conditions at epoch 150; it is not evidence of spontaneous learning order. The paper also describes standard-training and backward-correction curves under noisy-label conditions, including that models learned patterns first. No results test fitting completely random labels, unstructured inputs, training-time overhead for random labels, the full label-noise sweep in V4, or the necessity or sufficiency of the listed regularizers.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own noisy-label training curves and explicitly interprets the early improvement followed by test-accuracy decline as learning patterns first. These results bear on V6, although learning order is assessed indirectly through test accuracy.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate, but the main conclusion is that SIGUA improves robustness by selectively counteracting undesired memorization in self-teaching and backward correction. Patterns-first learning is an empirical observation motivating that intervention.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies noisy-label learning and selective gradient ascent, not the original experiment of training standard networks on completely random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with the base learning method, dataset, and noise type. In the motivating experiment, results also depend on the deliberately changed good/bad-data conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: After true labels identify corrupted examples at epoch 150, SIGUA makes both networks forget 99% of flipped labels and raises test accuracy from 23% to 95%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Oracle-guided gradient ascent can erase previously memorized corrupted labels and improve clean-test accuracy in this MNIST experiment.

record.problems: The motivating true-label experiment deliberately defines good and bad data and changes those conditions during training, limiting its relevance to spontaneous learning order. Most curve results are figure-only in the supplied text; individual values and uncertainty estimates are not stated there.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error and chance test performance under unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters. The 80% corruption experiment retains label signal.
Training-time overhead relative to clean labels and convergence speed as corruption increases. Comparing wide and deep networks at one noise level does not establish either.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit across increasing corruption fractions and a test-error trajectory toward chance. The reported test-accuracy comparisons do not establish this joint claim.
Whether the listed regularizers prevent random-label fitting, and whether removing them harms clean-label generalization.
A direct comparison of completely random versus real labelings, and quantitative separation of clean-example and corrupted-example learning order in the main experiments.

missing.what: Standard-training trajectories on CIFAR-100 and NEWS under all three noise conditions. Appendix B reports a trend similar to Figure 2. Preserve the reported later recovery on CIFAR-100 when recording trajectories.
missing.locator: Appendix B, Figure 4 and accompanying discussion

missing.what: Backward-correction trajectories on CIFAR-100 and NEWS under all three noise conditions. Record the baseline trajectories separately from SIGUA's mitigation performance; the text reports accuracy decreases but does not explicitly establish learning order for every panel.
missing.locator: Appendix B, Figure 5 and accompanying discussion

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. Main-experiment V6 support rests on the authors' explicit interpretation of test-accuracy curves, rather than direct measurement of when individual noisy labels are memorized. The oracle intervention in Figure 1 begins after standard training and should not invalidate observations from its earlier phase, but the endpoint outcomes in R5 and R6 do not measure learning order.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels, near-zero training error, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time for random versus true labels and convergence versus corruption fraction.
Shuffled, independently permuted, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
A sweep from clean to completely corrupted labels with perfect training fit and steadily rising test error.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or augmentation prevent random-label fitting, or whether removing them harms generalization.
The paper studies noisy labels rather than completely random labels, and does not directly compare learning on real versus random labelings.
